title: CuS Nanosheet Arrays for Electrochemical CO2 Reduction with Surface Reconstruction and the Effect on Selective Formation of Formate
abstract: Copper-based catalysts have shown excellent performance in electrochemical CO2 reduction, but there has not been much study on copper sulfides. In our work, a simple and low-temperature chemical bath deposition method was used to fabricate CuS nanosheet arrays on brass, on which a Faradaic efficiency over 70% and a production rate over 50 mA·cm−2 for formate were obtained at a low potential of −0.7 V vs RHE when used as a catalytic electrode for CO2 reduction. During the CO2 reduction process, CuS nanosheets were partially reduced to Cu and reconstructed to a nanowire network. It was found that residual S beneath the Cu layer lowered the binding energies of intermediates HCOO* and *COOH, promoting their desorption and the successive formation of HCOOH or HCOO−, thus regulating the high selectivity of the product. This work provides a convenient and economical method for developing a highly active electrocatalyst for producing HCOOH in CO2 electroreduction, and it is beneficial to understand the mechanism of enhanced selectivity to HCOO− for CuS electrode materials.

KEYWORDS: CO2 reduction, electrocatalysis, CuS nanosheet arrays, formate, brass mesh
■ INTRODUCTION In recent years, the increasing global temperature and sea level has become an indisputable fact, and the main reason is the enormous emission of greenhouse gases, which has reached the highest level in human history. The tremendous consumption of natural fossil fuels results in large CO2 emission which causes serious environmental problems, and the fixation of CO2 relative to emission amount is small. To improve this unbalanced carbon cycle and find alternatives for fossil fuels are urgent tasks faced by human beings.1−3 Electrochemical reduction of CO2 occurs under mild conditions, which can be carried out at normal temperature and pressure. Moreover, electrical energy for electrochemical reduction can be provided by renewable energy, for instance, wind and tidal energy, finally realizing an effective carbon cycle.4 In addition, electrocatalytic methods are clean and energy sustainable, and products can be used as fuel for the present energy infrastructure. Recently, considerable research on CO2 electrocatalytic reduction has occurred. However, some challenges to the electrochemical reaction still exist. The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is the main competitive reaction to the electrochemical reaction of CO2 reduction.
5,6 Meanwhile, multiple products and intermediates are produced during CO2 reduction through a multiple number of proton-coupled electron transfer steps, resulting in a low selectivity of products.7,8 In addition, the CO2 molecule is highly
thermodynamically stable and kinetically impeditive, causing an inactivated CO2 molecule.
9,10 Therefore, the critical need in CO2 electrocatalytic reduction research is to design and find electrocatalysts that can inhibit the HER, with a low overpotential and effectively promoting the CO2 reductive reaction, simultaneously, with merits of low cost, high selectivity, high stability, and durability. Cu-based electrocatalysts have aroused great research
interests for CO2 reduction. However, Cu shows an impractical overpotential requirement and high activation of the HER, inducing low selectivity for CO2 electroreduction.
11,12 Many other elements have been used to tune the electronic structure of electrocatalysts to improve catalytic reduction efficiency and selectivity, such as copper alloys or copper modified by nonmetallic elements.13−19 Copper sulfide (CuS) is a transitional metal sulfide with low cost and high earth abundance and presents properties such as metallic-like conductivity and narrow band gap. battery cathode materials, aluminum ion batteries, and photocatalysts have been studied widely.20,21 However, there is limited research of copper sulfides in CO2 electroreduction. It has been reported that CuS nanosheet arrays grown on nickel foam (CuS@NF) exhibited a high selectivity for CH4 with a long-term stability, but it was only elucidated experimentally.22 It also has been reported that particle size and initial sulfur content of sulfur-modified copper catalysts (Cu−S) affect the selectivity, and a high electron efficiency (FE) of HCOO− was achieved around 80% at −0.8 V vs RHE.23 It was corroborated experimentally and theoretically by operando Raman spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) that the presence of sulfur on a copper surface affects the adsorption strengths of HCOO* and *COOH intermediates of the HCOO− product, and CuSx showed an FE(HCOO−) of 75% at −0.9 V vs RHE.22 On the basis of previous works, CuS as the electrocatalyst in CO2 reduction exhibits high catalytic activity to yield formate. However, combining the experimental processes, especially the specific structural changes with the theoretical study, has been inadequate. Herein we report a cost-effective and facile method to
fabricate CuS nanosheet arrays on brass mesh (BM) (CuS/ BM), adopting a one-step chemical bath process. Twodimensional (2D) nanosheet materials possess abundant electroactive sites and shorten the length for transport of ions and electrons.24,25 In addition, brass is a kind of bimetallic alloy of Cu and Zn and has advantages of corrosion resistance and being abrasion proof and inexpensive. For example, a similar CuSn alloy has shown local corrosion during the CO2 reduction reaction and alternation of catalytic activity.19 The unique shape of brass mesh is conducive to the diffusion of CO2. Furthermore, the copper in brass mesh can react with polysulfide, and the zinc in brass mesh affords mechanical coherence and is difficult to react with polysulfide.26 Therefore, it ensures a better-controlled 2D-nanosheet structure of the samples when the substrate is brass mesh rather than copper alone. The as-synthesized nanosheet arrays of CuS were examined as electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction and exhibited an enhanced selectivity for HCOO−. During the reduction process, in situ Raman spectroscopy, ex situ Raman, XPS, and HRTEM were adopted to analyze the reconstruction of CuS/ BM and the mechanism of selectivity toward HCOO−. Further DFT calculation explored the binding energies between CO2, *COOH, HCOO*, and Cu or Cu/CuS, and results were compared with characterization results to speculate on the reaction mechanism.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Materials. All reactants in the experiment were of analytical grade and were not further purified. Na2S·9H2O (Macklin), S powder (Alfa), absolute alcohol (Beijing Chemical Works), KHCO3 (Alfa), concentrated hydrochloric acid (Beijing Chemical Works), and PTFE dispersion (Alfa) were all analytical reagents purchased commercially. Brass mesh (200 mesh) with 64% copper content and 36% zinc content was provided by Daoguan Rubber & Plastic Hardware, Inc., Shanghai.
Fabrication of CuS/BM. CuS/BM was fabricated through a chemical bath deposition method. As depicted in Scheme 1, a piece of brass mesh (size: 3 × 4 cm2, 200 mesh) was thoroughly cleaned in ethanol and distilled water, respectively, by ultrasonic pretreatment. CuS nanosheet arrays/BM were obtained through corrosion in polysulfide solution, consisting of Na2S (0.1 mol·L
−1), S (0.1 mol· L−1), and NaOH (0.1 mol·L−1). The brass mesh was immersed into the solution (50 mL) and maintained at 30 °C for 24 h. The asprepared samples were washed several times with distilled water and ethanol. Finally, the samples were dried at 60 °C for 8 h.
Characterizations. X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns of the samples were recorded on a Shimadzu XRD-6000 powder X-ray diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 Å) at 40 kV and 40 mA, and the instrument was operated at a scan rate of 10° per min in the 2θ range from 10° to 80°. The morphology and crystal structure of CuS/BM were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss SUPRA 55) at a voltage of 20 kV and by high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM, JEM-2010) at a voltage of 200 kV both connected to energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Raman spectra of catalysts were obtained with a Renishaw inVia Raman spectrometer using a 532 nm line of a He−Ne gas laser as the excitation source, and the in situ Raman spectroscopy test (Figure S1) used a quartz window electrolytic cell (Beijing Science Star Technology Co., Ltd., China). The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out on a Thermo VG ESCALAB 250 X-ray photoelectron spectrometer with Al Kα radiation at a pressure of about 2 × 10−9 Pa, and all the binding energies were referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV.
Electrochemical CO2 Reduction Performance Tests. Electrochemical measurements were carried out on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation (CH Instruments Inc., Shanghai) with a gastight H-type cell. Thirty milliliters of electrolyte (0.5 mol·L−1 KHCO3) was poured into cathodic and anodic compartments, which were separated by a Nafion 115 membrane. CO2 gas (99.999%) was continuously flowed through the electrolyte at a flow rate of 40 mL·min−1 for 20 min before the electrolysis, and the pH of the electrolyte reached 7.2. CuS/BM was used as the working electrode (1 cm × 1 cm). A Ag/ AgCl electrode (3 mol·L−1 KCl) was used as the reference electrode, and a graphite rod was used as the counter electrode. The potentials in the study were referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) by the following equation:

Products Analyses. The gas products were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC7920) with a TDX-01 column, and N2 was used as carrier gas. CO and CH4 were detected by a flame ionization detector (FID). H2 was detected using a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). Liquid products were analyzed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (AV600 600 MHz NMR) with water suppression using a presaturation method. Products were analyzed after reduction of CO2 at various overpotentials for 90 min. Theoretical Calculation. DFT calculations were adopted to analyze the binding strength between CO2, reaction intermediates, and catalyst surface. The structure optimization was carried out with CASTEP using Materials Studio. Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with a Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) functional was employed. All models adopted the LDA+U method with a Cu 3d U value of 4.5 eV. An energy cutoff of 489.8 eV, a k-point separation of 0.03 Å−1, and a self-consistent field (SCF) tolerance of 2 × 10−6 eV per atom were set. The Brillouin zone sampling adopted 1 × 3 × 1 kpoints.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Structure of As-Prepared Catalysts. The XRD pattern (Figure S2a) of the substrate indicates that the brass mesh corresponds to Cu0.64Zn0.36 (JCPDS no. 06-0464). SEM and HRTEM (Figure 1a and Figure 1c) exhibit hexagonal
nanosheet morphology for CuS/BM with an average diameter of ∼1 μm and thickness of 30−40 nm. The nanosheet arrays are uniformly grown on the surface of the brass mesh through one-step chemical immersion. The element mapping results (Figure 1b) reveal that the S, Cu, and Zn elements are uniformly distributed on the surface of the catalyst. The loading amount of CuS (0.54 ± 0.03 mg·cm−1) is calculated by the mass difference value before and after the preparation of materials with the EDS result (Table S1). The HRTEM images of CuS/BM (Figure 1d) indicate a good crystal form of the CuS nanosheet. The ordered lattice spacings are clearly observed with lattice spacings of 0.19 and 0.27 nm, which
agree well with the (110) and (006) facets of CuS, respectively.27,28 The peaks in the Raman spectrum diagram of CuS/BM appearing at about 143.9, 264.8, and 474.7 cm−1
(Figure S2b) correspond closely to those reported in the Raman spectrum of the CuS crystal. The strong peak at 475.0 cm−1 was attributed to the characteristic stretching vibration of the S−S bond.21,29 XPS analysis of CuS/BM agrees well with the Raman result. The spectra of S 2p (Figure S2c) depict that the peaks at 161.6 and 162.6 eV are assigned to S 2p3/2 and S 2p1/2, respectively.
30 The peaks (Figure S2d) at 932.3 and 952.1 eV are assigned to Cu0 2p3/2 and 2p1/3 in the brass substrate, while peaks at 934.2 and 954.2 eV are assigned to Cu2+ 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 in CuS arrays, respectively. The other peaks at 941.7, 943.9, and 962.8 eV correspond to the shakeup satellite peaks of Cu2+. These characterizations confirmed the formation of CuS.
Electrochemical Reduction of CO2. Based on the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) shown in Figure 2a, the curve of CuS/BM in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte manifests a lower onset potential of −0.25 V compared with CuS/BM in Ar. At the current density of 20 mA·cm−1, CuS/ BM shows a lower potential (−0.45 V) compared with brass mesh (−0.74 V) and copper mesh (−0.74 V) in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte, indicating that CuS/BM is active for CO2 reduction. Considering the oxidation and dissolution of platinum at high potentials, a graphite rod is used as the counter electrode and a proton exchange membrane is used to prevent the cross-contamination of cathodic and anodic compartments. The LSV tests using a graphite rod and platinum foil as counter electrode are compared in CO2saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a sweep rate of 10 mV· s−1 in a gastight H-type cell as shown in Figure S3, and the test results are the same, indicating that it makes no difference whether platinum or graphite is used as the counter electrode. As shown in Figure 2b, chronoamperometry of CuS/BM is assessed for 90 min at potentials over the range of −0.1 V to −0.8 V. It is notable that CuS/BM achieved a remarkable initial current density of 75 mA·cm−2 at −0.7 V, and the current increased slightly with time. When the potential was lower than −0.7 V, slight shedding of active material was observed, which caused the current decay. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analyses (Figure S4a−c) demonstrate that the as-fabricated CuS/BM shows a small interfacial charge transfer resistance (Rct) of 0.95 Ω at −0.7 V after 1 h of CO2 reduction compared with the substrate, indicating a fast charge transfer rate to promote the catalytic property of the CO2 reduction process.
31 In Figure 2c, a large double-layer capacitance (Cdl, 2.19 mF·cm
−2) of CuS/BM is obtained, showing a large electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) for CO2 reduction compared with that of the brass mesh substrate (1.54 mF·cm−2) and copper mesh (0.84 mF· cm−2), and their cyclic voltammetry (CV) plots in Ar-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 at different scan rates are shown in Figure S4d− f. The ECSA analysis is provided in Table S2. The product analysis results (Figure S5) show that HCOO−, CO, CH4, and H2 are detected throughout all potentials. The FE for HCOO− reaches the maximum value of 67.8 ± 1% at −0.7 V. FEs of CO and CH4 (Figure S6) are both lower than 1% and can be negligible relative to HCOO−. Consequently, it is concluded that CuS/BM is highly selective toward HCOO−
formation. The surface modifier PTFE controls reaction kinetics and product selectivity due to the turn of electrode surface from aerophobic to aerophilic, causing the promotion

of CO2 adsorption and the limitation of proton supply. 32 CuS/ BM modified with PTFE (0.5 μL·cm−2) produced HCOO− effectively with an FE of 70.2 ± 1% at −0.7 V (Figure 2d). The comparison for the reported main products of the copperbased electrode modified by sulfur is plotted in Figure 2e, and the detailed data are listed in Table 1. For production of HCOO−, CuS/BM achieved an FE of 70.2 ± 1% at a low potential of −0.7 V. The comparison of FEHCOO− for CuS/BM, brass mesh, Cu mesh, and CuS formed directly on Cu mesh (Cu mesh is vulcanized in 0.01 mol·L−1 Na2S, 0.01 mol·L
−1 S, 0.01 mol·L−1 NaOH for 5 min) is shown in Figure S7, which follows the order CuS/BM > CuS on Cu mesh > brass mesh > Cu mesh in terms of FEHCOO− at −0.7 V. The cycle test with 20 cycle numbers is processed to evaluate the stability of CuS/BM (Figure 2f). At each iteration, electrolysis is sustained for 1.5 h at −0.7 V in the closed electrolytic cell, and before every electrolysis, CO2 is flowed through the electrolyte at a flow rate of 40 mL·min−1 for 20 min. Apparently, the FE of HCOO−
experiences an increase before the first eight cycles, and the last cycle shows a negligible degradation relative to the first cycle. The average FE of 20 tests is 71.4 ± 1%. It is indicated that CuS/BM was stable after the initial rapid reconstruction. Mechanism for the Formation of HCOO−. Because a
transformation on the surface of the electrode occurred during the initial electrocatalytic reaction, the surface compositions
and valence states of elements, the morphology, and crystal structure of CuS/BM were investigated by XPS, Raman, and HRTEM analyses. In Figure 3a, the first cycle LSV curve in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a sweep rate of 10 mV·s−1 shows a redox peak at −0.25 V, which is attributed to the reduction of CuS to Cu. The redox peak disappears in the second LSV cycle, and curves after the second cycle are the same. To further investigate the reconstruction of the electrocatalyst, in situ Raman, ex situ Raman, and XPS analyses of CuS/BM and CuS/BM after the CO2 reduction LSV test of 0 to −0.25 V, the LSVs at 0 to −0.5 V and 0 to −0.75 V were carried out, and the results are in accordance with the reduction of CuS to Cu. The in situ Raman test is carried out along with the LSV in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The spectra (Figure 3c) show the attenuation of the S−Cu band and S−S bond, and finally a weakened Raman signal of the S−S bond remains, indicating that partial CuS is reduced to Cu. In the ex situ Raman spectra (Figure 3b), Cu2O and CuO phases occurring with the increase in cutoff voltage are attributed to the exposure of the reduced electrode to air. The reduction of CuS is also demonstrated by the XPS results, as shown in Figure 3d. The peaks at 932.3 and 952.1 eV are assigned to Cu0 2p3/2 and 2p1/2, which are lower than the binding energies of pure Cu, because the substituting Cu at the sublayer with S caused a

decreased coordination number of Cu around S and weakened the original chemical bonds around S.41 Meanwhile, the peaks at 934.2 and 954.2 eV are assigned to Cu2+ 2p3/2 and 2p1/2, respectively. The XPS analyses of S 2p are shown in Figure S8. Further XPS analysis shows a rising trend in the area ratio of Cu0/Cu2+, indicating a decrease of the CuS phase. Figure S9 shows the relationship of the area ratio of Cu0/Cu2+ with the cutoff voltage. A higher peak position variation (0.8−2.3 eV) of Cu2+ in Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 is attributed to the transfer of CuS to CuO via the oxidation of the reduced copper. As shown in Figure 4a−d, SEM images of CuS/BM after the CO2 reduction LSV test manifest a reconstruction of the electrocatalyst from nanosheet arrays to nanowire. By analysis of the products, the highest FE of HCOO− is obtained at −0.7 V. To further explore the changes of the crystal and the mechanism, in Figure 4e, HRTEM images of CuS/BM after the CO2 reduction LSV tests under 0 to −0.25 V, 0 to −0.5 V, 0 to −0.75 V, and 0 to −1.0 V are provided. The interplanar distance on the edge of the sample shows a value of 0.20 nm with a crystal plane angle of 90°, which agrees well with the Cu(111) plane. The characteristic of the interplanar distance (0.30 nm) is not in conformity with CuS. It is speculated that Cu2O is formed by the reduced electrode in contact with air, and the interplanar distances of 0.30 nm with 60° and 90° correspond to the CuS(102) plane and the Cu2O(110) plane, respectively.42−44 The results are in accordance with Raman and XPS results. It has been reported that the Cu(111) plane is prone to produce HCOO−.45 It has been verified that the surface binding of the carboxyl intermediate is very weak on Cu(111) plane compared with Cu(110) and Cu(100) via DFT calculation, which indicates that HCOO− production is enhanced on the Cu(111) plane.41,46 Furthermore, it has been reported that Cu(111) doping with element S affected the production of HCOO−, and DFT calculation shows that the presence of S weakened the adsorption energies of HCOO* and *COOH, which suppressed the further
formation of CO and facilitated the production of HCOO−.37 Furthermore, the FEs of products for the substrate at −0.7 V are provided in Table S3, which show high FEs of CH4 (11.7%), CO (49.9%), and H2 (35.8%), and only a little HCOO− is produced. The FEs of different products on the brass mesh substrate demonstrate that the substrate is not the active material for HCOO− production. This has been verified in the literature.47 It has been reported that different potentials had little effect on HCOO− production of CuxZn (x = 2, 4, 10). Therefore, the selective formation of HCOO− for CuS/ BM was attributed to the Cu(111) plane and the presence of S species. The result confirmed that S species in CuS and the reduced Cu played significant roles in HCOO− production. HCOOH is a product of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 with great economic benefit, which is economically viable with a net present value of $39.4 million under current technical and economic conditions.48 It has been proposed that chemical fixation of CO2 to afford HCOOH as a CO2 reduction product ranks only second to H2C2O4 and CO in emission reduction. 49 These are the proposed reaction mechanisms representative of HCOOH and CO:

The binding energies between the corresponding intermediates (*COOH and HCOO*) and the electrocatalysts affect the reaction selectivity for HCOOH. Lower binding energies of *COOH and HCOO* promote the formation of HCOOH, which are attributed to the easy desorption of the intermediates. DFT calculation was adopted to analyze the binding strength between CO2, reaction intermediates, and catalyst

surface. For the formation of HCOOH, a strong adsorption of CO2 is needed to facilitate the activation of catalyst, while low *COOH and HCOO* binding energies are expected to desorb easily from the surface of catalyst. Three-dimensional atomic models of the Cu(111) plane and Cu(111)/CuS(102) adsorbed with CO2, HCOO*, *COOH, and HCOOH are shown in Figure 5a−j. The binding energies of the molecules on the Cu(111) plane and Cu(111)/CuS(102) surfaces are compared. Detailed numerical calculation is provided in Tables S4 and S5. The binding energies of CO2 molecules on the Cu(111) plane (−2.06 eV) and Cu(111)/CuS(102) surface (−2.07 eV) are comparable, manifesting similar adsorbed states of CO2 on the two surfaces. For the comprehensive evaluation of the influence of Cu(111) on CuS(102), the free energy diagrams for reducing CO2 to HCOOH, CO, and H2 on Cu(111) and Cu(111)/CuS(102) are shown in Figure 5k− m. In Figure 5k, Cu(111)/CuS(102) shows a lower uphill of HCOO* to *HCOOH by 0.87 eV than that of Cu(111), because HCOO* exhibits stronger adsorption on Cu(111) (−3.83 eV) than that on Cu(111)/CuS(102) (−2.27 eV). For the *COOH pathway, in Figure 5l, the binding energy of *COOH on the Cu(111) plane (−3.58 eV) is lower than that on Cu(111)/CuS(102) (−2.95 eV), indicating that the desorption of *COOH is enhanced on Cu(111)/CuS(102) compared with the Cu(111) plane, promoting the formation of formate. Meanwhile, the existence of CuS inhibits the adsorption of *CO on Cu(111)/CuS(102) (−2.55 eV)
other than Cu(111) (−8.98 eV). In addition, a stronger adsorption of *H (Figure 5m) on Cu(111)/CuS(102) (−3.20 eV) reduces the activity for the HER.
■ CONCLUSION In this study, a facile and energy-saving method was applied to fabricate CuS nanosheet arrays on brass mesh with a one-step chemical bath deposition reaction. Benefiting from the 2D nanosheet array structure on BM, CuS/BM used as the electrode for CO2 electroreduction enhanced the activity for the generation of HCOO−. CuS/BM showed large total current density as high as 75 mA cm−2 at −0.7 V vs RHE coupled with an FE of 67.8 ± 1% for HCOO−, while an FE of 70.2 ± 1% for HCOOH/HCOO− at −0.7 V vs RHE was observed when CuS/BM was coated with PTFE. During the reduction process, the structure of CuS/BM underwent initial reconstruction, which formed a highly disperse nanowire network with multiple active sites. With the effective integration of experimental and theoretical study, the high selectivity toward HCOO− production was ascribed to the reconstructed formation of Cu(111)/CuS(102) during the reduction process. It was found that S beneath the Cu0 layer lowered the binding energies of HCOO* and *COOH on Cu(111)/CuS(102) compared with Cu(111) plane, which facilitated the formation of HCOOH or HCOO−. This work is beneficial to the development of effective electrocatalysts for the production of HCOO− in CO2 electroreduction. It also
